stories.headline: Update: Broncos linebacker Jonathon Cooper pleads not guilty to felony assault in domestic violence case
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos linebacker Jonathon Cooper entered a not guilty plea Monday to a felony assault charge for allegedly strangling his ex-girlfriend, along with several lesser charges, in Douglas County District Court. Cooper, 28, appeared alongside his attorney Harvey Steinberg but did not speak during the hearing. Judge Daniel Warhola set Cooper's trial for Nov. 10, 12 and 13.

Steinberg argued for a speedy trial, citing the case's "very negative impact on my client's ability to make a living." Cooper was placed on the NFL commissioner's exempt list Sunday, meaning he can attend meetings and work out at the facility but cannot practice or play in games. The Broncos are scheduled to play nine regular-season games before the trial begins.

Cooper was first arrested June 5 on a felony assault charge alleging strangulation of his now-former girlfriend, then again June 12 for violating a protection order after sending her 20 unreturned messages and knocking on her apartment door. He subsequently spent more than a month at an inpatient clinic near Vail before reporting to training camp July 29. The NFL has not yet determined whether Cooper will face a suspension under the personal conduct policy.

stories.headline: Broncos fill out 17-man practice squad, lose TE Justin Joly and nickel Reese Taylor to Dolphins on waivers
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos completed their 2026 practice squad Monday, signing four veterans including offensive lineman Calvin Throckmorton, but suffered unexpected losses on the waiver wire when the Miami Dolphins claimed tight end Justin Joly and nickel back Reese Taylor. Joly, a fifth-round pick out of UConn and North Carolina State, was the highest-drafted player from Denver's 2026 class to be waived. Head coach Sean Payton said the team had expected Joly to clear waivers and return to the practice squad.

The Broncos' 17-man squad includes an exemption for international player and outside linebacker David Agoha. Day 3 draft picks safety Miles Scott and linebacker Red Murdock cleared waivers and returned to the practice squad. Running back Jaleel McLaughlin, whom Payton called the toughest cut of the roster reduction, was weighing options with other teams as of Monday.

Payton noted that special teams performance was a key factor in several roster decisions, including the choice to keep running backs who contributed on coverage units. The Broncos have now lost a pair of players to waivers in each of the past three seasons, a recurring challenge when attempting to move young players through to the practice squad.

stories.headline: Avalanche sign Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche have signed defenseman Cale Makar to a contract extension worth $163.2 million, the largest in NHL history. The deal surpasses previous records and locks up the cornerstone of Colorado's blue line for the foreseeable future. Makar, widely regarded as the best defenseman in the game, has been central to the Avalanche's recent success including their 2022 Stanley Cup championship.

The signing underscores the Avalanche's commitment to building around their core nucleus for the long term. Makar has won the Norris Trophy as the league's top defenseman multiple times and finished among the top scorers league-wide each of the past several seasons. The contract will have significant salary cap implications for the franchise as it attempts to maintain a competitive roster around Makar, Nathan MacKinnon, and Mikko Rantanen.

stories.headline: Colorado voters to decide Proposition 137, which would redirect sporting goods sales tax to conservation and wildfire mitigation
stories.summary:
State election officials have approved signatures to place Proposition 137 on the November ballot, a measure that would redirect $175 million to $180 million a year in existing sales taxes on sporting goods equipment toward conservation, wildfire mitigation, watershed restoration and outdoor recreation. The measure would nearly double annual funding for Great Outdoors Colorado by allocating $83 million to $85.6 million annually, while directing more than $83 million a year to wildfire risk mitigation split evenly between the Colorado Department of Natural Resources and the State Forest Service.

Colorado currently spends only about $16.4 million a year on wildfire reduction and $5 million on burned landscape rehabilitation — figures proponents say are far short of what is needed. The Colorado Office of Outdoor Recreation Industry and Colorado Parks and Wildlife's Outdoor Equity Grant Program would each receive about $4.5 million annually under the measure. Colorado Parks and Wildlife has identified $900 million in capital needs over the next five years.

GOCO director Jackie Miller called the ballot measure potentially the most significant conservation vote since the 1992 statewide measure that created GOCO itself, which has invested $1.7 billion in more than 5,900 projects statewide. Proponents note the measure does not impose new taxes but rather redirects existing revenue already collected at the register. If approved, it would represent a tenfold increase in the state's wildfire mitigation spending.

stories.headline: Front Range Passenger Rail board votes to put sales tax measure on November ballot for southern expansion
stories.summary:
The Front Range Passenger Rail board has voted to place a sales tax measure on the November ballot to fund expansion of passenger rail service along the southern Front Range corridor. The measure represents a major step toward creating a long-envisioned rail network connecting Colorado communities along the I-25 corridor. If approved by voters, the revenue would help finance construction and operations of the southern segment of the proposed line.

The project has been under discussion for years as Colorado's population and traffic congestion along the Front Range have grown significantly. Passenger rail advocates argue the corridor is one of the most logical alignments for intercity rail in the Mountain West. The board's decision sets up what could be one of the most consequential transportation votes in Colorado in a generation.

stories.headline: Denver street takeover at 10th and Broadway draws no arrests, renews calls for tougher laws
stories.summary:
A street takeover at East 10th Avenue and North Broadway disrupted a Denver neighborhood late Sunday night, with cars doing donuts, lighting fireworks and blocking traffic as other drivers honked trying to get through. Denver Police said officers from the street racing team responded but that participants had dispersed by the time they arrived. No arrests were made and no citations were issued, the third such incident on or near Broadway this summer.

Nearby resident Micaiah Lambright said the noise became uncontrollable around 10:30 p.m. and that the events appear to be migrating closer to the city's core. He and other residents say the recurring incidents undermine Mayor Mike Johnston's vision of a more residential downtown. Similar takeovers have occurred at Broadway and Mississippi earlier in August and on Federal Boulevard in July.

State Rep. Chad Clifford, a Democrat from Arapahoe County, co-sponsored legislation last session to create escalating penalties for stunt driving and classify coordinated street takeovers as a Class 6 felony, with fines, license suspension and potential vehicle impoundment. The bill died in committee after concerns that its definitions were too broad and could unfairly target cultural groups such as lowrider communities. Clifford says existing statutes are not well-suited to address the organized nature of modern street takeover events.

stories.headline: Colorado teen arrested after posting viral 'Cat in the Hat' school threat meme on social media
stories.summary:
A 14-year-old Grand Junction High School student was arrested Monday after posting a social media message implying that a person dressed as the "Cat in the Hat" would appear at a local middle school and random homes, Grand Junction Police said. Officers determined there was no credible threat but arrested the student on suspicion of interference with staff, faculty or students of educational institutions. The arrest follows a nationwide social media trend in which AI-generated and real images of people in Cat in the Hat costumes are used to imply threatening visits to schools and neighborhoods.

Police said the posts are "intended to cause alarm and fear" and that investigators are actively monitoring the trend. Denver Public Schools said Monday it was not aware of any reports of the trend in the district, while Jeffco Public Schools said officials were aware but had received no specific concerns. The trend mirrors the 2016 "killer clown" scare, during which Colorado students in Greeley were arrested for posting threats on social media.

The Cat in the Hat trend has generated thousands of videos on TikTok, many of them AI-generated depictions of the character lurking outside windows and in driveways. Authorities in Colorado and nationally are warning that participation in the trend, even without a credible underlying threat, can result in criminal charges.

stories.headline: Denver Museum of Nature & Science opens $20 million Sturm Family Wing with renovated historic entrance and new lobby
stories.summary:
The Denver Museum of Nature & Science is reopening its historic east entrance after a four-year, $20 million renovation funded largely by the Sturm Family Foundation — the largest private donation in the museum's history. The new Sturm Family Wing features a redesigned lobby, upgraded large-format theater, covered outdoor plaza with new seating and landscaping, and accessible ramps connecting the main staircase area to the museum's atriums. A ribbon-cutting ceremony was scheduled for Tuesday morning, Sept. 1, followed by a free public grand opening from 4 to 9 p.m.

The renovation took place in two phases, with the first upgrading the theater including a new flat stage and a hearing loop system connecting directly to hearing aids and cochlear implants. The second phase expanded the lobby by removing former office space, added a built-in bar accessible during evening events, and created new outdoor dining and gathering areas. Officials said the outdoor plaza will be open from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily.

The grand opening evening will include the Denver premiere of "Penguins: A Love Story" and a screening of "T. Rex 3D" in the newly named Sturm Infinity Theater, along with live science demonstrations, hands-on activities and live music. Museum admission will be free all evening, with theater tickets sold separately. The project represents the museum's most significant expansion since the Space Odyssey exhibit was redesigned in 2020.

stories.headline: Denver Water's viral 'hole' billboard campaign raises drought awareness with $686,000 ad push
stories.summary:
Denver Water has launched a $686,000 marketing campaign featuring 22 billboards and 21 bus shelter ads across the city that cross out the water-related portion of common phrases — displaying "hole" instead of "watering hole" and "boy" instead of "water boy" — to highlight the region's ongoing drought. The campaign, designed by Denver-based Sukle Advertising & Design, has gone viral on social media as residents debate whether the minimalist messaging is clever or confusing. Denver Water's public affairs director Stacy Chesney said the goal is to make residents pause and think about their water use.

Denver Water's reservoir system is currently only 73 percent full, compared to a typical level of 94 percent at this time of year. Officials project reservoirs could drop to 60 percent full before next spring's runoff arrives. The utility recently implemented new drought restrictions requiring Denver Water's 1.5 million customers to shut off lawn sprinklers at the start of October.

The campaign has attracted national social media attention, with TikTok videos about the billboards drawing thousands of views and hundreds of comments. Denver Water said the attention is exactly what it hoped for, using the viral moment to direct people to its website for indoor and outdoor water-saving resources. Officials say the summer of 2026 has been the warmest on record for metro Denver.

stories.headline: Edgewater's experiment with Colorado's new tipped wage law offers cautious relief for restaurants, uncertainty ahead
stories.summary:
Edgewater became the only municipality in Colorado to utilize a 2025 state law allowing a wider tip credit, freezing tipped worker pay at $13.50 an hour for 2026 rather than implementing a planned $1.67 raise. The move has saved Edgewater Inn owner Niya Gingerich an estimated $30,000 this year, but she says the savings only allowed her restaurant to maintain the status quo rather than grow, as expenses across the board have risen. Edgewater City Council is scheduled to discuss next year's tipped wage rate Tuesday.

If the city takes no action before year's end, the freeze will expire and tipped workers' pay will jump $3.32 an hour — a 25 percent overnight increase — on Jan. 1, 2027, when Edgewater is also scheduled to match Denver's broader minimum wage of $19.84 an hour. Other Edgewater restaurant and bar owners echoed Gingerich's experience, saying the freeze helped them avoid raising menu prices but did not produce meaningful profits. Some workers expressed surprise at Colorado's tipped wages compared to states like Virginia and Texas, where the federal tipped minimum of $2.13 still applies.

The experiment offers an early look at how Colorado's relatively new tipped wage flexibility law functions in practice. Supporters of higher tipped wages argue the lower rate still leaves workers dependent on customer generosity in an era of rising living costs, particularly in the Denver metro area. The Edgewater council's decision Tuesday will shape whether the city extends, modifies or allows its tip credit policy to lapse heading into 2027.

stories.headline: Australian café chain Two Hands to open second Denver location in Cherry Creek
stories.summary:
Two Hands, the Australian restaurant and café chain with a location on Tennyson Street in Berkeley, will open a second Denver spot this spring at 221 N. Milwaukee St. in Cherry Creek, on the ground floor of BMC Investments' The Oasis apartment building. Founder and CEO Henry Roberts said the 3,400-square-foot space will feature much of the same core menu as the Berkeley location — known for brunch items including Piri Piri Chicken and a peach scramble — along with a new street-facing coffee window and a 900-square-foot patio. Roberts signed a 10-year lease.

The Cherry Creek interior will be designed to feel more upscale than other Two Hands locations, with a fireplace included in the space. BMC CEO Matt Joblon said the restaurant fills a gap in Cherry Creek's breakfast and brunch options, particularly since Syrup closed nearby. Roberts said his Tennyson location doubled its revenue to $4 million in 2026 and that the company projects $25 million in group-wide sales this year.

Two Hands, which Roberts founded in New York City in 2014, now operates eight locations across New York, Texas, Tennessee and Colorado. Roberts said he aims for at least three stores per market and is searching for a third Denver location, though no lease has been signed. The chain is founder-led with no outside investment backing its expansion.

stories.headline: Death of Englewood Mayor Pro Tem on Quandary Peak prompts review of high-altitude medical warning signs
stories.summary:
Englewood Mayor Pro Tem Joe Anderson, 45, died Aug. 28 after collapsing on the lower slopes of 14,272-foot Quandary Peak in Summit County, according to the Summit County Sheriff's Office. Lifesaving measures were attempted but unsuccessful. Anderson was known for his work on homelessness solutions, affordable housing, infrastructure and bicycle-pedestrian safety in Englewood. His cause of death has not been officially determined but appears to be medically related.

Anderson's death has prompted Colorado outdoor health experts to highlight the early warning signs of medical distress at altitude, including general fatigue, headaches, nausea, shortness of breath, chills and impaired sweating. At high elevation, the combination of altitude stress and summer heat can accelerate dehydration and overexertion. Experts recommend slowing down, hydrating and consuming calories at the first signs of distress, and strongly encourage turning back toward the trailhead if symptoms do not subside.

For altitude sickness specifically, descent is the only reliable treatment, and catching it early typically provides rapid relief. Hikers are advised to carry satellite communication devices in areas without cellular service and to hike with partners who can make clearer decisions if one member becomes impaired. The incident is a reminder of the risks even on well-traveled Colorado peaks during what has been an unusually hot summer.

weather.notable: Nearly 6 degrees above the average high for this time of year.

joke.joke: Before you criticize a man, walk a mile in his shoes. That way, when you do criticize him, you'll be a mile away and have his shoes.

topStory.headline: Nepal Puts Reconstruction Cost at $5 Billion After Glacial Flood Kills 939, Leaves Thousands Missing
topStory.summary:
A catastrophic glacial flood that struck northern Nepal along the Tibet border last week has killed at least 939 people and left nearly 4,500 others missing, Nepali officials confirmed. The disaster began on Aug. 26 when part of a glacier collapsed on the China-Nepal border, sending a massive wave of ice, rock and water down the Bhote Koshi River valley in the Rasuwa district, temporarily damming the Lhende River before the barrier gave way and unleashed a powerful flood downstream.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah, a rapper-turned-politician elected earlier this year, declared the flood 'not an ordinary' event and attributed it directly to climate change, calling on the international community to take action. 'This incident indicates that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change,' Shah said in a late-night social media post on Aug. 31. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters that initial estimates place reconstruction costs for the hardest-hit Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts at up to $5 billion, a figure he said would be considerably less than the $9 billion spent following the country's devastating 2015 magnitude-7.8 earthquake, which killed 9,000 people.

Rescuers were still working through day seven of search operations as of the latest reports, with some 538 of those missing identified as foreign nationals. Adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing hazards have complicated efforts to reach affected areas, according to government officials. Nepal has a population of roughly 30 million people, the vast majority living in rural conditions with limited national resources to mount a response at this scale.

Scientists and international bodies have long warned that glaciers across the Himalayan and Hindu Kush mountain systems are melting at an accelerating rate as global temperatures rise, increasing the frequency and severity of glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and debris flows. Glaciers in the broader region serve as a critical water source for an estimated 240 million people in the mountains and another 1.65 billion people in the river valleys of South and Southeast Asia. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned during a 2023 visit to Nepal that Himalayan regions were struggling with rapidly melting glaciers, and UN climate chief Simon Stiell described the Aug. 26 disaster as a 'devastating reminder of how fragile these mountain environments can be.'

Nepal, which has contributed negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions, is positioning the disaster as a test case for international climate accountability and loss-and-damage financing. Prime Minister Shah said the time had come to 'strongly raise' Nepal's situation with the global community, framing the recurring disasters as consequences borne by a poor nation for pollution generated largely by wealthier, industrialized countries. A full damage assessment remains ongoing, with officials cautioning that the final toll in lives and infrastructure could rise further.
